title: What is Blue-Green deployment vs Canary deployment vs Rolling deployment — Blue-Green (two identical environments, switch traffic all at once), Canary (send small % of traffic to new version first, increase gradually), Rolling (replace instances one by one) — and when do you use each?
shortTitle: Blue-Green vs Canary vs Rolling deployment, and when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: These are three deployment strategies that trade off risk, speed, cost, and rollback ability. Blue-Green runs two identical environments — the current blue and the new green — and switches all traffic from blue to green at once, giving instant cutover and instant rollback at the cost of double the infrastructure. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first and increases the share gradually while watching metrics, limiting blast radius so a bad release affects few users. Rolling replaces instances of the old version with the new version a few at a time until all are updated, needing no extra environment but mixing versions during the rollout and offering slower rollback.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India upgrading its branch systems. Blue-Green is building a second identical branch next door with the new system, testing it, then redirecting all customers to it in one switch — and if anything is wrong, switching everyone straight back. Canary is quietly sending just a handful of customers like Rajesh to the new counter first, watching closely, and only if all goes well sending more and more until everyone is on it. Rolling is upgrading the counters one at a time while the branch stays open, so at any moment some counters are new and some are old until the last one is done.
s1_definition.oneliner: Blue-Green switches all traffic at once between two full environments for instant cutover and rollback; Canary shifts a small, growing percentage to limit blast radius; Rolling replaces instances a few at a time with no extra environment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are three deployment strategies that trade off risk, speed, cost, and rollback ability. Blue-Green runs two identical environments — the current blue and the new green — and switches all traffic from blue to green at once, giving instant cutover and instant rollback at the cost of double the infrastructure. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first and increases the share gradually while watching metrics, limiting blast radius so a bad release affects few users. Rolling replaces instances of the old version with the new version a few at a time until all are updated, needing no extra environment but mixing versions during the rollout and offering slower rollback.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India upgrading its branch systems. Blue-Green is building a second identical branch next door with the new system, testing it, then redirecting all customers to it in one switch — and if anything is wrong, switching everyone straight back. Canary is quietly sending just a handful of customers like Rajesh to the new counter first, watching closely, and only if all goes well sending more and more until everyone is on it. Rolling is upgrading the counters one at a time while the branch stays open, so at any moment some counters are new and some are old until the last one is done.

**One line to remember:** Blue-Green switches all traffic at once between two full environments for instant cutover and rollback; Canary shifts a small, growing percentage to limit blast radius; Rolling replaces instances a few at a time with no extra environment.

sections.s2_technical:
Blue-Green keeps two complete environments. The blue environment serves production while you deploy and fully test the new version in green. When green is verified, you flip the router or load balancer so all traffic goes to green at once; blue stays warm as an instant rollback target. The strengths are a clean cutover with no version mixing, instant rollback by flipping back to blue, and the ability to test green thoroughly before any user hits it. The costs are roughly double the infrastructure during the switch and the need to handle stateful concerns such as database migrations carefully so both environments agree on schema. You use Blue-Green when you need instant, clean cutover and rollback, for example for a critical release where you cannot tolerate a slow or messy rollback, and when you can afford the temporary double capacity.

Canary releases the new version to a small slice of traffic first — say one or five percent — while the rest stays on the stable version, and you watch error rate, latency, and business metrics. If the canary is healthy you increase the share in steps to twenty-five, fifty, and a hundred percent; if it regresses you route everyone back to stable, so only the small canary slice was ever exposed. The strengths are the smallest blast radius of the three and the ability to validate on real production traffic gradually, often automated with tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger that promote or abort based on metrics. The costs are added complexity in traffic routing and metric analysis, and a longer total rollout time. You use Canary when the risk of a regression is high or the change is significant, when you serve enough traffic that a small percentage is still a meaningful sample, and when you want automated, metric-driven promotion with minimal user impact.

Rolling replaces the old version with the new one incrementally: it starts a few new instances, waits for them to become healthy, then terminates a few old ones, repeating until the fleet is fully updated. It is the default in Kubernetes Deployments, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, which govern how many extra instances can run and how many can be down during the rollout. The strengths are no extra environment and no big capacity spike, so it is cost-efficient and simple. The costs are that both versions serve traffic simultaneously during the rollout, which requires backward compatibility between versions and between the app and the database, and rollback is slower because it is itself a rolling operation back to the old version. You use Rolling for routine, low-to-moderate-risk updates of stateless services where brief version mixing is acceptable and you want simplicity and no extra cost.

A senior nuance ties them together. The right choice depends on risk tolerance, cost budget, statefulness, and how fast you must roll back. Blue-Green is best when instant rollback and clean cutover justify double cost; Canary is best when you want the smallest blast radius and metric-driven confidence on real traffic; Rolling is best for everyday low-risk changes where cost efficiency and simplicity matter most. Across all three, database schema changes must be backward and forward compatible — using expand-and-contract migrations — because at some moment old and new code may both be running, and feature flags often complement these strategies by decoupling the code deployment from the feature activation so you can turn a feature on gradually or off instantly regardless of which deployment strategy delivered the code.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India deploys three services with different risk profiles: a critical payments service needing instant rollback, a new fraud-scoring model needing cautious gradual exposure, and a routine account-query service needing a simple cost-efficient update. We want a deployment coordinator that applies the right strategy per service and can roll back.

Problem 1 — The payments service cannot tolerate a slow rollback, so we use Blue-Green: deploy green, flip all traffic, keep blue warm for instant revert.

Problem 2 — The fraud model is risky, so we use Canary: shift one, then ten, then fifty, then a hundred percent while watching metrics, aborting to zero on regression.

Problem 3 — The account-query service is low risk, so we use Rolling: replace instances a few at a time with no extra environment. Our runnable Java simulation models a `DeploymentStrategy` interface with `BlueGreen`, `Canary`, and `Rolling` implementations and a `DeploymentCoordinator` that runs the chosen strategy and reports traffic and rollback behavior. Classes: `DeploymentStrategy`, three strategies, `DeploymentCoordinator`, and a `DeploymentStrategyDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the Java demo
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.deploy.DeploymentStrategyDemo

# Real Kubernetes equivalents
# Rolling (default Deployment):
kubectl set image deployment/account-query app=account-query:1.5.0   # maxSurge/maxUnavailable control pace
# Canary/Blue-Green via Argo Rollouts:
kubectl argo rollouts set image fraud-scoring app=fraud-scoring:2.0.0
kubectl argo rollouts promote fraud-scoring     # or 'abort' on regression
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three releases — payments via Blue-Green, fraud via Canary (which will regress), and account-query via Rolling.

Step 1 — The coordinator releases payments-service 3.0.0 with Blue-Green: it deploys green beside blue and tests green with no live traffic, then flips all traffic from blue to green at once and keeps blue warm so rollback would be an instant flip back.

Step 2 — The coordinator releases fraud-scoring 2.0.0 with Canary. It shifts one percent, then ten percent, watching metrics.

Step 3 — At the fifty percent step the canary metrics regress, so the strategy aborts immediately and routes all traffic back to the stable version, meaning only the small canary slice was ever exposed to the bad model.

Step 4 — The coordinator releases account-query 1.5.0 with Rolling across six instances, two at a time, so after each batch more instances run the new version while the rest still run the old, requiring backward compatibility, until all six are updated with no extra environment.

Step 5 — Each strategy logged its distinctive behavior: Blue-Green's clean flip and instant rollback, Canary's graduated exposure and safe abort, and Rolling's incremental in-place replacement — illustrating why the choice depends on risk, cost, and rollback needs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Blue-Green, Canary, and Rolling are three deployment strategies that trade off risk, cost, speed, and rollback ability, and I choose between them based on the service's risk profile and how fast I must be able to roll back. Blue-Green runs two identical environments, the current blue and the new green; I deploy and fully test green with no live traffic, then flip all traffic from blue to green at once and keep blue warm as an instant rollback target. Its strengths are a clean cutover with no version mixing and instant rollback, and its cost is roughly double the infrastructure during the switch plus careful handling of database migrations, so I use it for critical releases where I cannot tolerate a slow or messy rollback and can afford the temporary double capacity.

Canary releases the new version to a small slice of traffic first, maybe one or five percent, while everyone else stays on stable, and I watch error rate, latency, and business metrics; if it is healthy I increase the share in steps to twenty-five, fifty, and a hundred percent, and if it regresses I route everyone back to stable so only the canary slice was ever exposed. It has the smallest blast radius of the three and validates on real production traffic gradually, often automated with Argo Rollouts or Flagger that promote or abort on metrics, at the cost of more complex routing and a longer rollout, so I use it when a change is risky or significant and I serve enough traffic that a small percentage is still a meaningful sample. Rolling replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, which is the Kubernetes default controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable; it needs no extra environment and no big capacity spike, but both versions serve traffic during the rollout so it requires backward compatibility, and rollback is slower because it is itself a rolling operation, so I use it for routine, low-to-moderate-risk updates of stateless services.

In my project at the National Bank of India I applied all three deliberately: the critical payments service used Blue-Green for an instant flip and instant rollback, the risky new fraud-scoring model used Canary and was automatically aborted back to stable when metrics regressed at the fifty percent step so almost no customers saw the bad model, and the routine account-query service used a simple Rolling update with no extra cost. A senior point I always add is that across all three, database schema changes must be backward and forward compatible using expand-and-contract migrations because old and new code may run at the same moment, and feature flags complement these strategies by decoupling code deployment from feature activation, letting me turn a feature on gradually or off instantly regardless of how the code was delivered.

---

keyPoints: Rolling update: gradual replacement, zero downtime
Canary: small percentage first, then full rollout
Rollback: revert to previous version on failure
